subject: business
title: Blue Ocean Strategy: rebuild what buyers pay for, instead of fighting over the same buyers
dek: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne’s 2004 Harvard Business Review essay: stop matching rivals on the same factors in a crowded industry. Reconstruct the offer. Cirque du Soleil, Casella’s [yellow tail], and Nintendo’s Wii are the cases used here — only for facts named public pages actually state.

thumb.alt: Blue-and-yellow striped Cirque du Soleil big top standing on the Old Port waterfront in Montreal, with cranes and river behind it.

hero.alt: A large blue-and-yellow striped circus tent on Montreal’s Old Port, photographed in 2012, with the river and port cranes beyond the guy-lines.
hero.caption: Cirque du Soleil’s chapiteau at the Vieux-Port de Montréal, 5 May 2012. Kim and Mauborgne’s 2004 essay says Cirque kept and dressed the tent — the one circus object that still read as circus — while dropping the animal menagerie that had become costly and unpopular. This is a later touring tent, not a 1984 street pitch. The object is the point: a rebuilt circus, still under canvas.

honesty: This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a company biography and not a promise that “creating a new market” always works. Cirque du Soleil (1984) and [yellow tail] (U.S. launch, July 2001) did their work before the October 2004 Harvard Business Review essay named Blue Ocean Strategy. Kim and Mauborgne reconstructed those moves as exhibits. Nintendo’s Satoru Iwata stated an “Expansion of the Gaming Population” strategy in 2003, in his own words, before the essay; the 2013 INSEAD teaching case by Kim, Mauborgne, and Jason Hunter reads the Wii through their later grid. Claims about revenue multiples, case volumes, and ticket or console prices are taken from the named public pages cited in Read. Operating statistics those pages do not state are omitted. “Blue ocean” and “red ocean” are the authors’ metaphors. After the first explanation they are treated as labels for a reconstructed offer versus a crowded fight, not as scenery. The earlier Saturday capsule David and Goliath is named only where the Porter cost-versus-differentiation trade-off is the thing this essay tries to break. Southwest Airlines is not reused as a case.

timeline.label: Cirque du Soleil
timeline.detail: Guy Laliberté and a group of street performers founded Cirque du Soleil in Quebec. The 2004 HBR essay uses this company as its opening exhibit.

timeline.label: Value Innovation
timeline.detail: Kim and Mauborgne, “Value Innovation: The Strategic Logic of High Growth,” Harvard Business Review, January–February 1997. The earlier public statement: a leap in buyer value and a lower cost structure at the same time.

timeline.label: [yellow tail] in the U.S.
timeline.detail: Australia’s Casella Winery introduced [yellow tail] into the U.S. market. The INSEAD/HBR case abstract: first-year plan 25,000 cases; first-year sales nine times that.

timeline.label: Expansion of the Gaming Population
timeline.detail: Satoru Iwata, speaking later at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of Japan (7 December 2006): Nintendo set this as its basic strategy in 2003, after the Japanese console market declined from 1997 to 2003. The Nintendo DS was the first machine built for it.

timeline.label: The HBR essay
timeline.detail: Kim and Mauborgne, “Blue Ocean Strategy,” Harvard Business Review, October 2004. Cirque is the opening case. The book of the same title followed in 2005.

timeline.label: 25 million cases
timeline.detail: By the end of 2005, the INSEAD case abstract says, [yellow tail]’s cumulative sales were tracking at 25 million cases. The brand is described there as the fastest-growing in the history of the U.S. and Australian wine industries.

timeline.label: Wii ships
timeline.detail: Bloomberg, 13 September 2006: Wii priced at $249.99 in the U.S. (25,000 yen in Japan), on sale 19 November in the U.S. and 2 December in Japan. Iwata’s stated goal: enlarge the population of people who play, not out-horsepower Sony and Microsoft.

fun_fact.title: The NASA portrait is from 2009, not from Baie-Saint-Paul
fun_fact.text: Guy Laliberté flew as a spaceflight participant on Soyuz TMA-16 in 2009. NASA photographed him at a Johnson Space Center press conference on 23 July 2009, which is the portrait this capsule uses. That picture is a later biography fact. It is not evidence about 1984, and it is not a claim in the 2004 essay. Keep the street-performer founding and the spaceflight seat on different calendar lines.

glossary.explain: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne’s name for reconstructing an industry’s factors so that a firm creates new demand instead of fighting rivals for the same buyers. Public statement: Harvard Business Review, October 2004; book, 2005 (expanded 2015).
Kim and Mauborgne’s label for uncontested market space — an offer whose buyers are not already being fought over on the industry’s usual factors. A metaphor, not a body of water and not a guarantee.
Their label for a crowded existing industry: rivals benchmark one another on the same factors, and growth is a fight over share. The color is the authors’ image for bloody competition.

Kim and Mauborgne’s earlier name (HBR, January–February 1997) for a leap in buyer value and a lower cost structure at the same time. In the 2004 essay this is the mechanism inside a blue-ocean move. It is not “innovation” as a synonym for new technology.

glossary.term: Value Innovation: The Strategic Logic of High Growth
glossary.explain: Kim and Mauborgne, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1997. The public essay that named value innovation before the 2004 blue-ocean vocabulary.
Kim and Mauborgne’s four questions used to rebuild a value curve: which factors to eliminate, reduce, raise, and create. Written out as the ERRC grid.
The four-box worksheet for the Four Actions Framework. Eliminate and reduce cut cost. Raise and create lift buyer value. The official tools page works [yellow tail] as an example.

A simple chart: the industry’s competitive factors on the horizontal axis, the level at which each offer delivers them on the vertical. A new offer is a different line, not a higher copy of the old one. Developed in their earlier HBR work and used throughout the 2005 book.

People who could use the category but currently do not — because it is confusing, costly, intimidating, or aimed at someone else. The [yellow tail] and Wii cases are read as offers built for those people, not as better wine or a faster console for existing buyers.

Korean-born professor of strategy at INSEAD in Fontainebleau; co-director of the INSEAD Blue Ocean Strategy Institute. Co-author, with Renée Mauborgne, of the 1997 and 2004 HBR essays and of Blue Ocean Strategy.
Professor of strategy at INSEAD; co-director of the INSEAD Blue Ocean Strategy Institute. Co-author, with W. Chan Kim, of the essays and books this lesson uses.

Harvard Business School’s management magazine. The 1997 value-innovation essay, the 2004 blue-ocean essay, and the 2015 “Red Ocean Traps” piece all appeared here.

Quebec street performer (accordion, stilts, fire-eating, in the 2004 HBR lead) and co-founder of Cirque du Soleil in 1984. Later CEO. The NASA portrait in this lesson is from a 2009 spaceflight briefing, not from 1984.

Quebec entertainment company founded in 1984 by street performers including Guy Laliberté. Kim and Mauborgne’s opening 2004 exhibit: circus skills plus theater, without the animal menagerie, aimed at adults who would pay theater prices.

The large American circus the 2004 essay treats as the incumbent Cirque did not try to out-clown or out-lion. Named for the comparison of how long each took to reach a revenue scale; this lesson does not invent a later closing date from memory.

A late-twentieth-century European (especially French) current that treated circus as theater without animals: Cirque Plume (France, 1984) is a named peer of Cirque du Soleil’s founding year. Cirque did not invent theatrical circus alone.
French contemporary-circus company founded in 1984 — the same year as Cirque du Soleil. Named here so Cirque is not treated as the only troupe that dropped the menagerie and wrote a show.

Purpose-built circus arena in Shanghai (opened 1999). Placed in this lesson as a reminder that acrobatic spectacle in China was a state-supported and then commercial institution in the same decades Cirque was touring, not a footnote to Montreal.

Kyoto video-game company. Under Satoru Iwata it set “Expansion of the Gaming Population” as strategy in 2003 and shipped the Nintendo DS and then the Wii.

President of Nintendo from 2002 until his death in 2015. The 7 December 2006 FCCJ outline is the primary source this lesson uses for Gamer Drift and the 2003 population-expansion strategy. Photographed here at GDC 2011.

Nintendo designer (Donkey Kong, Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda). Bloomberg’s 13 September 2006 piece opens with his line that Nintendo has a machine even a mother could love. Named as a public voice, not as a secret strategist.

Nintendo home console, U.S. launch 19 November 2006, Japan 2 December 2006, $249.99 / 25,000 yen (Bloomberg, 13 September 2006). Motion controller, not a graphics race. Kim, Mauborgne, and Hunter’s 2013 case reads it as a noncustomer move.

The Wii’s one-handed motion controller. Iwata’s E3 2006 remarks compare it to the DS touch screen: a way to lower the barrier for people who would not pick up a many-button pad.

Iwata’s 2006 name for a shrinking player base: games took too much time and skill, and the gap between a first-time player and a veteran had become too wide. A Nintendo diagnosis, not a Kim–Mauborgne term.

Nintendo’s 2003 internal strategy phrase, as Iwata stated it in 2006: make products anyone can play regardless of age, gender, or gaming experience. “For 5 to 95 years old” and “the same start line” were the in-house lines he quotes.
Sony’s November 2006 home console, the high-definition, high-horsepower rival Iwata declined to match. Named as the industry path Nintendo did not take, not as a full Sony lesson.
Microsoft’s 2005 home console. With PlayStation 3, the graphics-and-online fight the Wii stepped beside.

Harvard Business School professor. Competitive Strategy (1980) treated cost leadership and differentiation as alternative generic strategies. Kim and Mauborgne’s value-innovation claim is that a reconstructed offer can pursue both at once. The earlier Saturday capsule David and Goliath is the Porter lesson in this archive.

Porter’s 1980 triad: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. Blue Ocean Strategy’s wager is that eliminate/reduce plus raise/create can deliver difference and low cost together. A claim, not a law.

The previous Saturday capsule in this archive: judo, disruption, and Porter, with Honda, Southwest, and Canon. Linked where the cost-versus-difference trade-off is the background. Southwest is not reused as a case here.

sections.title: When every rival improves the same list, the industry shrinks around that list

blocks.text: A crowded industry is easy to describe and expensive to live in. The firms already in it watch one another. They add the same features, bid for the same star performers or the same shelf talkers, and call the result strategy. Buyers who already like the category get a slightly better version of what they had. Buyers who never liked the category still have no reason to start. Costs rise because the shared list is costly to climb. Demand does not rise with it. Michael E. Porter’s generic strategies treated that bind as a choice: be cheaper, or be different, or do one of those in a narrow slice. The earlier Saturday capsule in this archive, David and Goliath, is the lesson that stays with Porter, judo, and disruption. This Saturday is the other claim: some firms stop climbing the shared list. They drop pieces of it, add pieces the list never included, and sell the result to people the industry had not been counting as customers.

W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, professors of strategy at INSEAD in Fontainebleau, gave that move a pair of names. In “Value Innovation: The Strategic Logic of High Growth” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1997) they called the mechanism value innovation: a leap in what buyers get, and a lower cost structure, in the same design. In “Blue Ocean Strategy” (Harvard Business Review, October 2004) they named the setting. A red ocean is the existing industry, rivals cutting one another on the same factors. A blue ocean is an offer whose demand is not already being fought over. The colors are theirs. The useful content is not the palette. It is the instruction to redraw the list of factors before you spend another year winning a point of share.

blocks.alt: Pale modern buildings of Cirque du Soleil’s international headquarters in the Saint-Michel district of Montreal, with a blue-and-yellow tent roof visible among the blocks.
blocks.caption: Cirque du Soleil’s international headquarters, Saint-Michel, Montréal, photographed in 2019. The 2004 essay’s opening firm became a large cultural exporter headquartered in this complex. The building is later than 1984. It is here as the address of a reconstructed circus, not as proof that a headquarters creates a market.

sections.title: Four questions, a grid, and a line that does not copy the industry’s line

blocks.text: The 2004 essay’s method is a short list of questions, later drawn as the Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create grid — the ERRC grid on the authors’ public tools page. Which factors that the industry takes for granted should be eliminated? Which should be reduced well below the industry standard? Which should be raised well above it? Which factors that the industry has never offered should be created? Eliminate and reduce cut cost. Raise and create lift what a new kind of buyer will pay for. If those four answers are real, the firm is no longer trying to be a cheaper circus or a more prestigious wine or a faster console. It is selling a different object. Kim and Mauborgne call the picture of that object a strategy canvas: the industry’s factors along the bottom, the level of each factor up the side, each offer a line. A reconstructed offer is a different line. It is not a higher copy of the old one.

Two warnings belong next to the grid, not at the end. First, the famous cases mostly predate the essay. Cirque du Soleil was founded in 1984. [yellow tail] reached American shops in July 2001. The October 2004 article is a reconstruction of moves already made. Nintendo is the partial exception: Satoru Iwata’s own 2003 phrase was “Expansion of the Gaming Population,” stated again in his 7 December 2006 outline for the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of Japan. Kim, Mauborgne, and Jason Hunter then wrote The Nintendo Wii: Lessons Learned from Noncustomers as an INSEAD case in 2013. Iwata was not holding their grid in 2003. He was naming a shrinking Japanese market and a product path that did not chase horsepower. Second, “noncustomers” is the people-word that makes the grid less abstract. The useful question is not what current buyers wish were slightly better. It is why a larger group refuses the category — confusion, price, intimidation, a sense that the product is for someone else — and whether an offer can be built that those people will actually use.

Value innovation is the load-bearing phrase from 1997, and it is stricter than it sounds. It is not a new gadget. It is not a brand campaign laid on top of the old cost structure. It is a change in the activity system that removes expensive factors buyers had been taught to expect and puts money into factors they did not have. That is how Kim and Mauborgne argue they escape Porter’s trade-off. Whether a given firm actually did both things at once is a fact question for each case. The grid is a way to ask the question. It is not a certificate.

blocks.text: Cirque du Soleil is the 2004 essay’s opening case, and it has to be read as a reconstruction. The open HBR page states the facts this lesson is allowed to use. Founded in 1984 by a group of street performers, Cirque had, at the time of the article, staged dozens of productions seen by some 40 million people in 90 cities. In twenty years, the essay says, it reached revenues that Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey — “the world’s leading circus” — had taken more than a century to attain. The magazine summary adds a 22-fold revenue rise over the previous ten years, in an industry the authors describe as in long-term decline. Those are 2004 sentences. They are not a 2020s income statement.

The strategic content is the rebuilt list. Traditional circuses, in the essay’s account, had been benchmarking one another: more famous clowns, more impressive animal acts, more of the three-ring split that raised cost without changing what a night at the circus was. Cirque stopped trying to be a better circus of that kind. It dropped the animal menagerie — training, veterinary care, transport, insurance, and a growing public objection — and it did not buy circus “stars” as the thing a ticket was for. It kept clowns and acrobatics, wrote a through-line closer to theater, commissioned original music, and dressed the tent instead of abandoning it for a rented hall. Ticket prices moved toward theater prices. The new buyers, in this reading, were adults and corporate clients who had not been going to the circus. Quartz’s 2015 restatement follows the same outline and does not add a figure this lesson will invent. Mystère (Las Vegas, 1993), Quidam (1996), and O (Bellagio, 1998) are later, checkable production titles. They show where the reconstructed circus was sold. They are not a second dataset.

blocks.caption: The Montreal chapiteau again, because the tent is the essay’s object: Cirque kept the one circus sign that still worked and spent on it. Ringling is not in the frame. The comparison in the 2004 essay is about time-to-revenue, not about this photograph.
blocks.credit: Jean Gagnon / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: [yellow tail] is the wine case, and it is a grocery object, not a château story. The public abstract of Crafting Winning Strategies in a Mature Market: The US Wine Industry in 2001 — Kim, Mauborgne, Jason Hunter, Brian Marks, Wayne Mortensen — states the setting and the volumes. In 2001 the U.S. wine trade was crowded, squeezed at distribution and retail, and still competing on factors that had barely moved in centuries: vineyard prestige, complexity, aging, the language of tannin and oak. In July 2001 Australia’s Casella Winery put [yellow tail] into that market. The firm had expected to sell 25,000 cases in the first year. It sold nine times that. By the end of 2005, cumulative sales were tracking at 25 million cases. The abstract calls it the overall best-selling 750 ml red, ahead of Californian, French, and Italian brands, and the fastest-growing brand in the history of the U.S. and Australian wine industries. Those sentences are the case authors’. This lesson does not add a later supermarket rank.

The rebuilt list, on the official ERRC teaching pages, is blunt. [yellow tail] stripped the factors wine had competed on — tannins, complexity, aging — and with them some of the working capital aging requires. It launched as two wines, a Chardonnay and a Shiraz, so a shopper who did not speak wine was not asked to perform a cellar. It was sold as a social drink for people who otherwise bought beer or a ready-to-drink cocktail. John Casella, in a SmartCompany interview, says the same thing in operator language: he was not going after the existing wine-drinking market; the $5.99 slot had more volume than the $8.99 wine he had already tried; W.J. Deutsch & Sons in New York was the distributor; the kangaroo-on-yellow label, in his account, rode a moment when Australia was easy to read in America after the Sydney Olympics. Deutsch’s first reaction, in that interview, was not enthusiasm. Distribution and a price point are part of the move. They are not a lesser footnote than the wallaby.

blocks.alt: Rows of grapevines on flat irrigated land near Griffith, New South Wales, with a farm shed and trees on the horizon under a hard blue sky.
blocks.caption: McWilliam’s vineyard at Hanwood, near Griffith, New South Wales, 26 July 2007. Casella is at Yenda, in the same Riverina irrigation district, not on this specific block. The photograph is the region the case comes from — bulk-capable, hot, flat — not a prestige slope and not a bottle shot.
blocks.credit: Willem van Aken / CSIRO / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 3.0

blocks.text: The Wii is the third case, and the primary voice is Iwata’s, not Kim’s. On 7 December 2006, at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of Japan, he put the diagnosis in the company’s own English outline. The Japanese video-game market had declined from 1997 to 2003 while North America was still growing. He called the domestic pattern Gamer Drift: games took too much time and energy, and the skill gap between a first-time player and a veteran had become too wide. Gorgeous graphics, he said, had reached a saturation point and would not enlarge the audience. In 2003 Nintendo set “Expansion of the Gaming Population” as its basic strategy — products for anyone regardless of age, gender, or gaming experience, with the in-house lines “for 5 to 95 years old” and “the same start line.” The Nintendo DS, with two screens, a touch screen, and a microphone, was the first machine. The Wii was the second, a new play style for the living-room console.

Bloomberg’s 13 September 2006 piece, “Nintendo: Wii Want To Expand Games’ Appeal,” is the contemporaneous price-and-date source. The Wii would sell for $249.99 in the United States (25,000 yen in Japan), on 19 November in the U.S. and 2 December in Japan. Shigeru Miyamoto’s line in that piece is that Nintendo has a machine even a mother could love. Iwata’s line is that the goal is to boost the population of gamers by making games for more people, against a market whose typical buyer was still being imagined as an 18-to-35-year-old man. In a May 2006 Associated Press interview, printed by the Orange County Register, Iwata said the race for horsepower and faster processing “don’t do anything to ask nongamers to play with a video game,” and that a controller bristling with buttons intimidated them. The 2013 INSEAD case by Kim, Mauborgne, and Hunter is a later classroom reading of those choices as an ERRC move aimed at noncustomers. It is useful as their reading. It is not a 2003 Nintendo memo.

blocks.alt: White Nintendo Wii console and Wii Remote displayed on black stands at the Electronic Entertainment Expo in 2006.
blocks.caption: The Wii as shown at E3 2006, photographed by Marcin Chady. The objects are a small white console and a remote that looks like a television clicker, not a many-button pad. This is the hardware of Iwata’s “same start line,” displayed months before the November U.S. launch. It is not a sales chart.
blocks.credit: Marcin Chady / Flickr / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0

sections.title: Other troupes, other cellars, other ways to enlarge a player base

blocks.text: Cirque du Soleil was not the only 1984 company that treated circus as theater without animals. Cirque Plume was founded in France that same year. It belongs to nouveau cirque, a current already underway in Europe: written shows, original scores, no menagerie, tents or rooms used as theaters. Archaos and other French companies followed. If Cirque is taught as a unique leap out of Ringling’s industry, the French calendar is the correction. The reconstruction was a period style, not a Montreal patent. In China the same decades kept a different institution: state-trained acrobatic troupes, then commercial houses such as Shanghai Circus World, the purpose-built arena that opened in 1999. That building is not “Asia’s Cirque.” It is evidence that acrobatic spectacle had another industrial history — training schools, municipal venues, tourist bookings — while Kim and Mauborgne were writing in Fontainebleau. The useful comparison is contemporaneous infrastructure, not a Western frame plus an Eastern peer.

blocks.alt: Cirque Plume’s striped touring tent and trailers in a winter field at Besançon, France, December 2016, with bare trees and a low pale sky.
blocks.caption: Cirque Plume at Besançon, 26 December 2016. Founded in 1984, the same year as Cirque du Soleil. A French contemporary-circus tent, not a subsidiary and not a copy in the case-study sense. The shared year is the point.

blocks.alt: The inverted-bowl dome of Shanghai Circus World at dusk, lit in changing colors, with a city overpass and traffic in the foreground.
blocks.caption: Shanghai Circus World, photographed 10 March 2010. Opened in 1999 as a permanent acrobatic house, not a touring chapiteau. Placed here as a 1990s–2000s Chinese venue contemporaneous with Cirque’s touring years and with the 2004 essay, not as a blue-ocean exhibit.
blocks.credit: Tom Page / Flickr / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0

blocks.text: Wine in 2001 was not only Napa against Bordeaux or Burgundy. Chilean Cabernet and Argentine Malbec were already moving through the same New World export boom that carried Australian wine into American grocery aisles. [yellow tail] is one branded reading of that boom — simple, fruit-forward, cheap to explain — not the boom itself. A strategy canvas that pretends the only alternative to French prestige was Casella’s wallaby is doing the West-plus-one trick this site refuses. The Riverina, the Central Valley, the Colchagua, and Mendoza were all producing high-volume wine for buyers who did not want a lesson. Casella’s move was to name that buyer out loud and to stop apologizing to the trade for it.

Games in 2003–06 had another expansion path that did not run through Kyoto’s living room. In South Korea, online titles and PC bangs had already pulled in players who did not own a Western home console. Lineage and later social and sports titles enlarged a population by the hour, in rented chairs, on a broadband network the Japanese home-console market did not use the same way. Iwata’s crisis figure was a declining Japanese console business from 1997 to 2003. A Korean internet café in those years was not in that decline. The Wii and the PC bang are not rivals in a case. They are two answers, in the same years, to the question of who gets to play and where the machine sits.

sections.title: A reconstructed offer can be copied, and a metaphor is not a test

blocks.text: Blue oceans fill in. Once a reconstructed offer is visible, rivals can take the easy pieces — a motion stick, a fruit-forward wine at $6, a circus without animals — and bolt them onto the old system. That is the Continental Lite problem from the Porter Saturday, in a new vocabulary. Kim and Mauborgne’s 2015 essay “Red Ocean Traps” is their own later warning: managers slide back into competing on the industry’s existing factors because those factors are easy to measure. The Wii’s motion idea was later copied in other living rooms. [yellow tail] did not remain the only cheerful Australian wine on an American shelf. Cirque’s theater-circus was imitated by other troupes and by Cirque’s own later, heavier slate of resident shows. The 2004 essay can describe a first move. It cannot keep a market empty.

There is also a hindsight problem the Honda files already taught. Cirque and Casella look like grid work after Kim and Mauborgne write the grid. Iwata looks like their student after the 2013 case. The honest order is the other way: the companies moved; the professors named a pattern; classrooms then treat the pattern as a kit a firm can pick up in advance. Sometimes that kit helps a later team ask better questions about noncustomers. Sometimes it becomes a slide that labels any successful product a blue ocean and any failure a red one. Survivorship is the ordinary vice of strategy writing. This lesson keeps the dates visible so the vice is harder to miss.

Value innovation’s claim against Porter is the other limit. Eliminate and reduce can lower cost. Raise and create can make a different offer. Whether those four answers, in a real firm, actually break the trade-off — or merely hide a cheap product behind new language — is not settled by a color. A simple wine at $5.99 is also a cost position. A console that refuses high-definition chips is also a cost position. Cirque’s theater ticket is also a differentiated price. The grid is still useful if it forces a team to name what it will stop doing. It is less useful if it is used to say that trade-offs were an illusion all along.

sections.title: The books continued; the companies did not stay in 2004

blocks.text: Kim and Mauborgne published the book Blue Ocean Strategy in 2005 and an expanded edition in 2015. Blue Ocean Shift followed in 2017, Beyond Disruption in 2023. “Red Ocean Traps” (HBR, March 2015) is the later essay this lesson uses as a caution. Cirque du Soleil grew into resident Las Vegas shows and a touring machine, then — years after the essay — into a leveraged entertainment group that had to halt live performance when a pandemic closed rooms. That later corporate history is not a 2004 fact and is not treated here as a secret ending hidden in the framework. [yellow tail] became a permanent grocery brand and a much larger Casella Family Brands. Nintendo’s next console after the Wii, the Wii U, is widely treated as a muddled follow-up; Iwata was still president for that launch. The 2003 sentence about enlarging the population outlived any one machine. The companies are evidence for a reconstructed offer. They are not saints, and they are not stuck on the year of the essay.

If you list the factors your industry already fights on, which two would you drop because buyers who are not yet customers do not use them — and what evidence, not a color, would tell you that you had built a different offer rather than a cheaper copy?
